items.title: The Night Nurse
text: Nadia had worked as a nurse for only three months, and tonight was her first night shift in the children's ward. At midnight the corridors were quiet, and the only sound was the soft hum of the machines. She walked from bed to bed, checking each small patient. In the last room, a six-year-old boy named Omar was awake. He was holding his teddy bear tightly, and his eyes were full of tears.

"I want to go home," he whispered. Nadia did not tell him to be quiet. Instead, she sat beside him and asked about his bear. Omar explained that it was called Sultan and that it was afraid of hospitals. Nadia smiled and said that Sultan could be her special patient too. She gently listened to the bear's heartbeat with her stethoscope and announced that it was perfectly healthy and only needed sleep. Omar laughed for the first time that night. A few minutes later, he was asleep.
When Nadia's supervisor passed by, she noticed the calm room and nodded proudly. "Medicine heals the body," she said quietly, "but kindness heals the rest."

qs.q: What is the best title for the passage?
o: A Dangerous Night in the Children's Ward
Nadia's Difficult Exams at Nursing School
A Teddy Bear That Became Seriously Ill
The Nurse Who Comforted a Frightened Boy
qs.e: The whole story is about how Nadia calmed a frightened child, so this title fits the main idea.

qs.q: Why did Nadia treat the teddy bear as a patient?
o: She wanted to practise using her stethoscope.
The supervisor had asked her to do so.
She wanted Omar to feel safe and less afraid.
qs.e: She joined Omar's game so that he would feel calmer. Later he laughed and fell asleep.

qs.q: The word "whispered" in paragraph 2 means ........
qs.e: At midnight in a quiet ward, Omar spoke softly. To whisper is to speak very quietly.

qs.q: What does the supervisor's last sentence suggest?
o: Nurses should never give children medicine.
Kind words are as important as medicine.
Children are happier at home than in hospital.
Night shifts are easy for new nurses.
qs.e: She says kindness 'heals the rest', so care for feelings matters as well as treating the body.

oq.q: Where was Nadia working on her first night shift?
oq.a: In the children's ward.

oq.q: What did Omar whisper to Nadia?
oq.a: "I want to go home."

oq.q: What does "it" in "it was afraid of hospitals" (paragraph 2) refer to?
oq.a: The teddy bear (Sultan).

oq.q: Why did Nadia treat Omar's bear as a patient? Explain in your own words.
oq.a: She wanted to comfort Omar and make him feel safe, so he would stop being afraid.
alt: To calm him down
Because she understood that a frightened child needs kindness
So that he would trust her and feel less afraid

oq.q: What does the supervisor mean by "Medicine heals the body, but kindness heals the rest"?
oq.a: Medicine cures illness, but kind words and care help people's feelings and fears.
alt: Doctors and nurses must also be kind, not only give medicine
Care for feelings is as important as treatment

items.title: Working with Machines
text: Many factories today use robots. A robot arm can lift heavy boxes, paint car doors, or tighten the same screw again and again without getting tired. Because machines do these repeated and sometimes dangerous jobs, workers are safer and products are often made faster.

However, machines cannot do everything. A robot does only what people have programmed it to do. If a new problem appears, it cannot think of a clever solution. Someone must also design the robot, repair it when it breaks, and check that it works correctly. For this reason, factories still need skilled people, especially people who understand computers and electricity.

Some workers worry that machines will take their jobs. It is true that certain jobs are changing. But new jobs are also appearing, such as robot technician and software designer. Experts advise young people to keep learning new skills, because the workers who can learn quickly will be able to work together with machines instead of competing with them.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Robots are too expensive for most factories to buy, so few use them.
Robots can think of clever solutions, so they will soon replace all workers.
Machines are useful, but people are still needed to design, control and repair them.
Workers should avoid computers and electricity because they are dangerous.
qs.e: The passage shows the benefits of machines and then explains that people are still necessary.

qs.q: According to the passage, why do factories use robots for some jobs?
o: The jobs are repeated or dangerous.
Robots can make decisions on their own.
Robots never need electricity or repair.
The workers are always too tired to work.
qs.e: Paragraph 1: robots do repeated and sometimes dangerous jobs, so workers are safer.

qs.q: The word "competing" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ........
qs.e: 'Work together with machines instead of competing with them' contrasts working together with trying to beat them.

qs.q: What does the writer advise young people to do?
qs.e: The last sentence says experts advise young people to keep learning new skills.

qs.q: Which job is mentioned as a NEW job?
qs.e: Paragraph 3 names 'robot technician' and 'software designer' as new jobs.

oq.q: Why can a robot not solve a new problem?
oq.a: A robot does only what people have programmed it to do.

oq.q: What do people still have to do for the robots?
oq.a: Someone must design the robot, repair it when it breaks, and check that it works correctly.

oq.q: Why does the writer say that factories "still need skilled people"? Answer in your own words.
oq.a: Because robots cannot think or solve new problems, so people must design, repair and check them.
alt: Robots depend on humans to work correctly
Machines cannot work alone

oq.q: Do you think the writer is for or against robots in factories? Give a reason from the passage.
oq.a: For, but with people: robots make work safer and faster, but people are still needed.
alt: He thinks they are useful but not enough alone
Positive, because robots make products faster and workers safer

oq.q: What can we learn about the future of jobs from the last paragraph?
oq.a: Some jobs change, new jobs appear, and people who keep learning will succeed.
alt: Learning new skills is the key to finding work
Jobs will change, not disappear

items.title: The River Clean-up
text: Behind Hana's school there was a small river that nobody liked to visit. Its banks were covered with plastic bags, old bottles and papers, and the water smelled bad. One morning, Hana's science teacher, Mr. Karim, showed the class photos of the same river taken many years ago. In the pictures, the water was clear and children were sitting happily under green trees.

"This place can be beautiful again," Mr. Karim said, "if we decide to care about it." The students made a plan. They asked their families for gloves and bags, and they invited their neighbours to help on Saturday. Over fifty people came. By the afternoon, they had filled more than thirty bags with rubbish.

The students did not stop there. They put up signs asking people to keep the river clean, and they planted small trees along the bank. A month later, Hana saw a white bird standing in the shallow water. "It came back," she said with a smile. "It was only waiting for us to do our part."

qs.q: Why did Mr. Karim show the class old photos of the river?
o: To show that the river was once clean and could be again
To teach them how to take good photographs
To prove that the river had always been dangerous
To ask them to move to a cleaner school nearby the town
qs.e: The photos showed the river clear and beautiful, so the students could believe it could change.

qs.q: How did the students get help for the clean-up?
o: They closed the school for a week.
They asked families and neighbours to join them.
They waited for the government to send help.
They paid workers to clean the banks.
qs.e: They asked their families for gloves and bags and invited neighbours to help on Saturday.

qs.q: What did the white bird in the last paragraph show?
o: The river was getting smaller every month.
The students were wasting their time on the river.
The river was becoming a better place for living things.
Birds like to sit on plastic bags and bottles.
qs.e: The bird returned only after the river became cleaner, a sign of success.

qs.q: Which word best describes Mr. Karim?
qs.e: He encouraged his students and made them believe in change, so he is inspiring.

oq.q: What was wrong with the river behind Hana's school?
oq.a: Its banks were covered with plastic bags, old bottles and papers, and the water smelled bad.

oq.q: What did Mr. Karim show the class?
oq.a: Photos of the same river taken many years ago.

oq.q: Why did the students ask their families for gloves and bags?
oq.a: To clean the river and fill bags with rubbish (they filled more than thirty bags).

oq.q: What does Mr. Karim mean by "if we decide to care about it"?
oq.a: The river can become beautiful again only if people make the decision and the effort to look after it.
alt: Change starts when people take responsibility
If we want it to be clean, we must work for it

oq.q: What did Hana mean by "It was only waiting for us to do our part"?
oq.a: The bird returned because people cleaned the river, so the river was safe again; nature recovers when we do our share.
alt: Nature comes back when we take care of it
The river needed our help

items.title: Gardens Under the Sea
text: Coral reefs are often called the gardens of the sea. They look like colourful rocks or plants, but corals are in fact tiny animals that live together in large groups. Over many years, they build hard structures that become homes for thousands of different kinds of fish, crabs and other sea creatures.

Coral reefs also protect people. Strong waves lose some of their power when they hit a reef, so coastal villages are safer during storms. In addition, many families depend on the fish that live around reefs for food and work.

Unfortunately, reefs are in danger. When sea water becomes too warm, corals can turn white and may die. Rubbish and chemicals that reach the sea can also harm them, and careless boats or divers can break them. Scientists say that we can help by using less plastic, keeping beaches clean, and never touching or standing on a reef when we swim. Small actions, repeated by many people, can give these underwater gardens a chance to survive.

qs.q: Why are coral reefs called "gardens of the sea"?
o: They look colourful and are full of life.
They are used to grow food.
They are made of real plants and flowers.
They grow only in gardens near the beach.
qs.e: The text says reefs look like colourful plants and are homes for many sea creatures.

qs.q: According to the passage, corals are ........
o: fish that build houses for crabs
a kind of colourful sea plant
rocks that never change or grow
tiny animals that live in groups
qs.e: Paragraph 1 says corals are in fact tiny animals that live together in large groups.

qs.q: How do coral reefs help people?
o: They weaken strong waves and provide food and work.
They clean the beaches after every big storm.
They keep boats away from the coast.
They make the sea warmer for fish.
qs.e: Paragraph 2 says reefs reduce the power of waves and many families depend on the fish for food and work.

qs.q: Which of these is NOT mentioned as a danger to reefs?
qs.e: Rain is not mentioned. Warm water, rubbish and chemicals, and careless boats or divers are.

oq.q: What are corals in fact?
oq.a: Tiny animals that live together in large groups.

oq.q: How do coral reefs protect people?
oq.a: Strong waves lose some of their power when they hit a reef, so coastal villages are safer during storms.

oq.q: Why can corals turn white and die?
oq.a: When sea water becomes too warm.

oq.q: Why does the writer call coral reefs "gardens of the sea"?
oq.a: Because they look like colourful plants or rocks and are home to many kinds of sea creatures, like a garden.
alt: Because many living things live in them
They look like beautiful plants

oq.q: How can small actions by many people help the reefs? Explain in your own words.
oq.a: If everyone uses less plastic, keeps beaches clean and does not touch reefs, together they reduce the harm and give the reefs a chance to survive.
alt: Many small efforts add up to a big result

items.title: A Mind That Can Grow
text: Have you ever said, "I am just not good at maths"? Many students think that ability is something we are born with, and that nothing can change it. Psychologists call this a fixed mindset. People with a fixed mindset often avoid difficult tasks because they are afraid of failing.

A growth mindset is different. People who have it believe that skills grow with practice, just like muscles grow with exercise. When they make a mistake, they do not give up. They ask, "What can I learn from this?" and they try a different way.

Think of a footballer who misses a penalty. A player with a fixed mindset may feel ashamed and refuse to take another one. A player with a growth mindset will practise more and take the next penalty bravely. In school, the same idea can help you with exams. If a question seems impossible, remember the word "yet": you cannot solve it yet. With patience and effort, you probably will.

qs.q: What does the writer compare skills to?
qs.e: Paragraph 2 says skills grow with practice, just like muscles grow with exercise.

qs.q: How does a person with a growth mindset react to a mistake?
o: He blames other people for it.
He feels ashamed and stops trying.
He avoids the task for ever after.
He learns from it and tries another way.
qs.e: They ask what they can learn and try a different way.

qs.q: Why does the writer mention the word "yet"?
o: To show that difficult tasks may become possible with effort
To show that the time of the exam is not important to anyone at all
To describe a rule that football players must follow
To say that some students will never learn a hard subject
qs.e: 'You cannot solve it yet' means you may be able to later with patience and effort.

qs.q: The word "fixed" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to ........
qs.e: A fixed mindset means believing ability cannot change.

oq.q: What do people with a fixed mindset often avoid? Why?
oq.a: They avoid difficult tasks because they are afraid of failing.

oq.q: What do people with a growth mindset ask when they make a mistake?
oq.a: "What can I learn from this?"

oq.q: What will a player with a growth mindset do after missing a penalty?
oq.a: Practise more and take the next penalty bravely.

oq.q: Why might a student with a fixed mindset avoid difficult tasks?
oq.a: Because he thinks his ability cannot change and he is afraid of failing.
alt: He is afraid of making mistakes
He believes he is not good enough

oq.q: What is the writer's message about mistakes and exams?
oq.a: Mistakes are chances to learn, and a hard question means "not yet"; with patience and effort we can succeed.
alt: Do not give up when something is difficult
We can improve with practice

items.title: Plans for Friday
text: On Thursday afternoon, four friends were trying to decide what to do on Friday. Salma wanted to see a new film at the cinema, but Youssef thought that was too expensive. Mona suggested a picnic in the park, and Ali, who was always quiet, only shrugged his shoulders.

"Ali, what do you think?" Salma asked kindly. Ali looked down. "I don't mind," he said. But Mona noticed that he was smiling when she talked about football in the park. "We can bring a ball, some sandwiches and a few board games," she said. "That costs almost nothing, and there is something for everyone."

Everyone agreed, even Salma, who promised that the cinema could wait until next month. The next day the weather was perfect. They played football until they were tired, ate their sandwiches under a big tree, and laughed over a long game of cards. When they walked home, Ali said quietly, "That was the best day I have had in a long time."

qs.q: Why did Youssef refuse the idea of the cinema?
qs.e: The text says he thought it was too expensive.

qs.q: How did Mona know that Ali liked the idea of the park?
o: He wrote his answer on a piece of paper.
He told her clearly in front of everyone that he wanted it.
He arrived early with a ball and sandwiches.
She saw him smiling when she mentioned football.
qs.e: Mona noticed he was smiling when she talked about football in the park.

qs.q: The word "shrugged" in paragraph 1 shows that Ali ........
qs.e: Lifting the shoulders usually means 'I don't mind' or 'I don't know'.

qs.q: What can we learn from Mona's plan?
o: The weather decides everything in the end.
A good plan can suit everybody and cost little.
Cinemas are bad places to spend a Friday afternoon.
Friends should never disagree about plans.
qs.e: Her plan had football, food and games, so there was something for everyone, at almost no cost.

oq.q: Why did Youssef not like Salma's idea?
oq.a: He thought the cinema was too expensive.

oq.q: What did Mona suggest?
oq.a: A picnic in the park.

oq.q: Why did Mona think her plan was a good one?
oq.a: It costs almost nothing, and there is something for everyone.

oq.q: What can we understand about Ali's character from the passage?
oq.a: He is quiet and shy, and he does not like to ask for things; he only shows what he likes by smiling.
alt: He is polite and does not want to cause problems
He is shy

oq.q: Why do you think Mona's plan pleased everyone? Answer in your own words.
oq.a: It was cheap and included something for each friend: football, food and games.
alt: Because it was good for every person
Everyone could enjoy it

items.title: The Missing Passport
text: Tarek was excited. It was his first flight, and he was going to visit his uncle in another country. At the airport, he checked in his suitcase, received his boarding pass and walked towards security. Then he put his hand in his jacket pocket and froze. His passport was not there.

He emptied his bag, searched every pocket and returned to the check-in desk, but nobody had seen it. His heart was beating fast and the boarding time was getting closer. A young woman in a yellow uniform noticed his worried face. "Can I help you?" she asked. When Tarek explained, she calmed him down and called the lost-property office.

Five minutes later, a cleaner had found a passport near the café where Tarek had bought a drink. It was his! The woman took him quickly to the gate, and he was the last passenger to board. As the plane took off, Tarek made a promise to himself: from now on, he would always keep his documents in one safe, zipped pocket.

qs.q: What was Tarek's problem at the airport?
o: He forgot his ticket at home.
He could not find his passport.
qs.e: He put his hand in his pocket and his passport was not there.

qs.q: Who helped Tarek?
o: A cleaner who was his friend
A woman in a yellow uniform
qs.e: A young woman in a yellow uniform noticed him and helped.

qs.q: Where had the passport been found?
qs.e: A cleaner found it near the café where Tarek had bought a drink.

qs.q: What did Tarek decide at the end of the story?
o: To arrive at the airport much later
To buy a new passport every single year
To keep his documents in one safe pocket
Never to travel by plane again
qs.e: He promised to keep his documents in one safe, zipped pocket.

oq.q: What did Tarek find when he put his hand in his jacket pocket?
oq.a: His passport was not there.

oq.q: How did the young woman help Tarek?
oq.a: She calmed him down and called the lost-property office.

oq.q: Where did the cleaner find the passport?
oq.a: Near the café where Tarek had bought a drink.

oq.q: How did Tarek feel when he could not find his passport? What shows this?

oq.q: What do you think Tarek learned from this experience?

items.title: Writing Before Paper
text: Long before there were notebooks and pens, people found other ways to write. In ancient Egypt, scribes were highly respected because they could read and write hieroglyphs, a system of pictures and signs. Few people had this skill, so scribes worked for kings, temples and traders.

The Egyptians also invented a light material for writing called papyrus. It was made from a plant that grew along the River Nile. Thin strips of the plant were placed in layers, pressed and dried to make sheets. Papyrus was much easier to carry than heavy stone, so messages, stories and records could travel farther.

Thanks to these ancient writers, we know a lot about how people lived thousands of years ago. Their writings, found in tombs and temples, tell us about their beliefs, their work and their daily lives. They remind us that writing is one of the most powerful inventions in history, because it allows one generation to speak to the next.

qs.q: Why were scribes respected in ancient Egypt?
o: They built the temples and tombs.
They could read and write, which few people could do.
They grew papyrus along the Nile.
They were rich traders and kings.

items.title: Looking at the Night Sky
text: On a clear night, far from the city lights, thousands of stars seem to cover the sky. People have looked at them for thousands of years and asked the same questions: What are they? How far away are they? Are we alone?

The invention of the telescope changed astronomy. A telescope collects light and makes distant objects look bigger and clearer. With it, astronomers could see the craters of the Moon and many stars that cannot be seen with the eyes alone. Today, powerful telescopes are even placed in space, where the air does not make the pictures blurry.

Still, much of the universe remains a mystery. Scientists continue to study how stars are born, why planets move as they do, and whether life exists elsewhere. The more they learn, the more new questions they find. This is what makes science exciting: every answer opens a new door.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Astronomers must now live in space to find answers about stars.
Telescopes and science help us explore the universe, but many mysteries remain.
The Moon is bigger than the Sun, so it is easier to study.

qs.e: The text moves from looking at the sky to telescopes and ends with unsolved mysteries.

qs.q: "Every answer opens a new door" means that ........

qs.e: The writer says the more scientists learn, the more new questions they find.

oq.q: What questions have people asked about the stars for thousands of years?
oq.a: What are they? How far away are they? Are we alone?

oq.q: What does a telescope do?
oq.a: It collects light and makes distant objects look bigger and clearer.

oq.q: Why are powerful telescopes placed in space?
oq.a: Because there the air does not make the pictures blurry.

oq.q: What does the writer mean by "every answer opens a new door"?

items.title: A Guest Is a Gift
text: One rainy evening, a car broke down near a small village. Inside were a family of four, tired and hungry, with no idea where to spend the night. A farmer named Hajj Mahmoud saw them from his door and walked quickly through the rain to offer help.

"Please come in," he said. "No one should wait outside in this weather." His wife prepared hot soup and fresh bread, and the children dried their clothes by the fire. Hajj Mahmoud called a mechanic from the next town, who promised to arrive in the morning. The mother tried to thank him many times, but he only smiled. "In our village, a guest is a gift from God," he said.

The next day the car was repaired. As they said goodbye, the father tried to pay for the food, but Hajj Mahmoud refused. "If you want to thank me," he said, "help the next stranger you meet." The family promised that they would, and the children never forgot the warm welcome of that rainy night.

qs.q: What did Hajj Mahmoud do to help?

He gave them food, a place to stay, and called a mechanic.
He repaired the broken car by himself that same night.
He asked them to wait outside until the rain stopped.
qs.e: He invited them in, his wife prepared food and he called a mechanic.

qs.q: What did he ask them to do in return?
o: Write him a letter of thanks
Come back to the village every year
Help the next stranger they meet
Pay him for the soup and bread
qs.e: He refused money and said to help the next stranger.

qs.q: What does "a guest is a gift" show about the village?
o: People there do not like visitors.
qs.e: It shows that hospitality is a value of the village.

oq.q: Why did Hajj Mahmoud walk through the rain?
oq.a: He saw a tired and hungry family whose car had broken down, and he wanted to offer help.

oq.q: What did Hajj Mahmoud's wife prepare for the family?
oq.a: Hot soup and fresh bread.

oq.q: Why did Hajj Mahmoud refuse the father's money?
oq.a: He wanted them to thank him by helping the next stranger they meet.

oq.q: What does Hajj Mahmoud's behaviour tell us about the people of his village?
oq.a: They are generous, kind and welcome strangers, even those they do not know.

items.title: Why We Read Stories
text: Why do people read novels, poems and plays? Some say literature is only for entertainment, but it does much more. When we read a story, we step into the life of another person. We feel his fear, we understand her choices, and we see the world through a different pair of eyes. This helps us to become more understanding and patient with people around us.

Literature also develops our language. Readers meet new words and ideas, and they learn how writers use description, dialogue and imagination to make a scene come alive. Many students find that after reading regularly, their own writing becomes clearer and richer.

Finally, great stories travel across time. A play written hundreds of years ago can still make an audience laugh or cry today, because the feelings it describes, such as love, jealousy and hope, belong to all people. In this way, literature is a bridge between different places and different centuries.

qs.q: According to the writer, how does reading stories help us?
o: It helps us understand other people better.
It stops us from ever feeling afraid again.
It makes us richer and more successful.
It makes us faster at solving maths problems.
qs.e: The passage says we step into another person's life and become more understanding.

qs.q: How can literature improve a student's writing?
o: By making the student write much less than he did before
By replacing grammar lessons completely at school
By giving ready-made answers to copy in exams
By teaching new words and how writers create scenes
qs.e: Paragraph 2 says readers meet new words and learn how writers create scenes.

qs.q: Why can an old play still touch modern audiences?
o: It describes feelings that belong to all people.
It is very short and easy to remember.
It is easy to understand without any effort.
It uses modern machines on the stage.
qs.e: Paragraph 3: love, jealousy and hope belong to all people.

qs.q: In the last sentence, "a bridge" means that literature ........
o: is difficult to cross for most young readers today
separates one culture from another culture
connects people from different places and times
is built of stone and takes years to cross
qs.e: A bridge connects two sides; here, different places and centuries.

items.title: Choosing a Career
text: Choosing a university subject or a future job is one of the biggest decisions young people make. Many students choose a subject because their friends choose it, or because it sounds impressive. This is not always wise.

A better way is to ask three questions. First, what do you enjoy doing? If you like helping people, medicine or teaching may suit you. If you enjoy building and solving problems, you might prefer engineering. Second, what are you good at? Look at your results and listen to your teachers' opinions. Third, what does the job market need? Some careers offer more opportunities than others, and this may change over time.

It is also useful to gain experience before deciding. You can speak to people who already work in the field, visit a workplace, or do a short summer course. Remember, too, that a first choice is not final. Many people change direction later and still succeed, because the skills they gained, such as communication, patience and teamwork, are useful in every career.

items.title: Learning First Aid
text: Accidents can happen anywhere: at home, at school or on the street. Knowing basic first aid helps us act quickly and calmly until professional help arrives. It does not replace a doctor, but it can prevent a small problem from becoming a serious one.

The first rule is to stay calm and make sure the place is safe for you and for the injured person. Then call for help or ask an adult to do so. For a small cut, wash your hands, clean the wound with clean water and cover it with a clean bandage. If someone feels faint, help him to sit down and ask him to breathe slowly.

Many schools and health centres offer short first-aid courses. A trained instructor can show you what to do and, just as important, what NOT to do. A person who learns these skills may one day help a friend, a family member or even a stranger.

items.title: Tea with Mrs. Fawzia
text: Every Friday afternoon, Salma went to an elderly care home near her house as a volunteer. She was only sixteen, and at first she felt shy. Most of the residents seemed to prefer watching television to talking to a teenager.

One day she sat beside Mrs. Fawzia, a quiet old lady who never smiled. Salma brought two cups of tea and asked, "Would you tell me about your school days?" Mrs. Fawzia looked surprised. Then she began to speak slowly. She had been a teacher for forty years, and she remembered every student's name. Salma listened for an hour without checking her phone.

When Salma stood up to leave, Mrs. Fawzia held her hand. "Nobody has asked me about my life for a long time," she said. "Thank you for listening." Walking home, Salma realised that she had given nothing but her time, and yet it had meant so much. From that day, she made sure that nobody in the home sat alone at tea time.

items.title: The Washing Machine
text: One Saturday morning, the washing machine in Karim's house stopped working in the middle of a wash. His mother was worried because the clothes were full of water, and she was about to call a repairman.

"Wait," said Karim. "Let me look at it first." He was studying electricity at school, and he loved solving technical problems. He unplugged the machine to be safe and watched a short video on his phone. Then he noticed that the small pipe at the back was blocked with a sock. He pulled it out, cleaned the pipe and plugged the machine in again. The water began to flow out immediately.

His mother laughed in relief and hugged him. "You saved us a lot of money," she said. Karim smiled, but he added, "I only did it because I unplugged it first. Safety always comes before repair." His mother nodded. She was proud that her son had learned not only a skill but also a good habit.

items.title: Smartphones: Friend or Enemy?
text: Smartphones have changed the way we live. With one small device, we can call a friend, look up a word, find our way in a new city or learn a new skill. For students, the phone can be a dictionary, a library and a classroom in one.

However, smartphones also have disadvantages. Many people spend hours scrolling through videos and messages without noticing the time. This can make it hard to concentrate on studying and can reduce the time we spend talking face to face. Some students find it difficult to sleep well when they use their phones late at night.

The solution is not to throw the phone away, but to use it wisely. You can set a time limit for games and social media, turn off notifications while you study, and keep the phone out of the bedroom at night. When we control the phone, it is a helpful tool. When it controls us, it becomes a problem.

items.title: Every Drop Counts
text: Water covers a large part of our planet, but the water that people can drink is limited. In many places, it is becoming harder to find clean water, so everyone should learn to save it.

Saving water starts at home. A tap that drips all day can waste a surprising amount of water, so it is important to repair leaks quickly. We can also close the tap while brushing our teeth, take shorter showers and wash vegetables in a bowl instead of under running water. The water left in the bowl can then be used for the plants.

Schools and communities can help too. Students can make posters to remind others to close the taps, and neighbours can share ideas for reusing water. These actions may seem small, but when millions of people do them, they make a big difference. Remember: clean water is not only a resource, it is a gift that we must protect for the next generation.

items.title: The Last Tree on Our Street
text: There was only one tree left on Yara's street, an old fig tree in front of the bakery. In the summer, its wide leaves gave shade to the people waiting for bread. One day, Yara saw a notice on the tree: it would be cut down to widen the road.

Yara felt sad, but she did not just complain. She talked to the baker, who agreed that the tree was important. Together they collected signatures from the neighbours and wrote a polite letter to the local council. They explained that the tree gave shade, made the air fresher and was home to many birds.

Two weeks later, a council engineer visited the street. After looking at the road, he decided to change the plan and widen the street on the other side instead. Yara and the baker could not hide their joy. That summer, the neighbours planted five new young trees beside the old fig. "A single voice can start a change," Yara told her little brother.

items.title: The Fisherman and the Net
text: Old Mahmoud had been a fisherman for forty years. Every morning, he left the harbour before sunrise and returned with a boat full of fish. But recently, he noticed that his nets were catching less fish and more plastic bags and bottles.

One day, while mending his net, he found a small turtle tangled in an old piece of rope. He cut it free carefully and watched it swim away. "The sea gave me my living all my life," he thought. "It is time to give something back."

From that day, Mahmoud brought a large bag on every trip and collected the rubbish he found. Soon other fishermen followed his example. items.title: A Responsible Day at the Beach
text: A day at the beach can be wonderful, but it can also harm the sea and the animals that live near it if we are careless. Responsible visitors follow a few simple rules.

First, take your rubbish with you. Plastic bags, cans and food packets can stay on the sand for a very long time, and animals may swallow them by mistake. Second, do not take living things such as shells with animals inside or small fish from the rock pools. They belong to their natural home. Third, be careful where you walk. Some areas of the shore are the nesting places of birds, and visitors may disturb them without realising it.

It is also wise to protect yourself. Use sun cream, drink plenty of water and swim only in places where it is safe and where a lifeguard is on duty. When everyone follows these rules, the beach remains clean, safe and enjoyable for the next visitors.

items.title: The Diver's Surprise
text: Adam had dreamed of diving since he was a child, and on his fifteenth birthday his uncle took him to the Red Sea for his first lesson. At first he was nervous. He felt the weight of the equipment on his back and listened carefully while the instructor explained the hand signals.

items.title: The Last Kilometre
text: Hassan was not a good runner. In his first school race, he finished last, and some of his classmates laughed. He felt embarrassed and decided to quit. But his sports teacher, Mr. Adel, spoke to him after the race. "Last place today does not mean last place for ever," he said. "Do you want to try again in three months?"

Hassan agreed. Every morning before school, he ran for twenty minutes. At first, his legs hurt and he had to stop often. Slowly, he could run longer. He also learned to breathe correctly and to rest well. When he felt like giving up, he remembered his teacher's words.

On the day of the next race, Hassan was nervous but ready. He did not win, but he finished in the middle of the group, and he had improved his time by almost four minutes. As he crossed the line, Mr. Adel was waiting. "I am proud of you," he said. Hassan smiled. For the first time, he understood that the real competition was with his old self.

items.title: Sleep, Food and Exams
text: During exam time, many students stay up late and drink a lot of coffee, believing that this will help them to study more. However, many experts say that good sleep and healthy food usually work better.

When we sleep, the brain has time to rest and organise what we learned during the day. A student who sleeps well can concentrate more easily and remember more. Food also matters. Breakfast gives the body energy for the morning, and fruit, vegetables and water help us to feel active. Too much sugar, on the other hand, may give a quick burst of energy that soon disappears.

Exercise is another useful habit. A short walk between study sessions can clear the mind and reduce stress. A good study plan, therefore, is not only about reading for many hours. It also includes enough sleep, regular meals and a little movement. Students who look after their bodies are often better prepared to face the exam.

items.title: How to Be a Good Friend
text: A true friend is someone you can trust, but friendship also needs effort from both sides. If you want to keep good friends, it helps to remember a few simple habits.

First, be a good listener. When a friend talks about a problem, try not to interrupt or to give advice too quickly. Sometimes people only need someone who listens. Second, be honest but kind. If you disagree, say it politely, because harsh words can hurt feelings that are not easy to repair. Third, keep your promises. If you say that you will come or call, do it. Trust takes a long time to build and only a moment to lose.

Finally, remember that friends are not perfect. Everyone makes mistakes, and sometimes we disagree. The important thing is to apologise when we are wrong and to forgive when others apologise. These habits will not only protect your friendships but also help you become a better person.

text: On the first day of the school year, a boy named Zaid stood alone at the school gate. He had moved from another city, and he did not know anyone. During the break, he sat on a bench and opened his sandwich without looking at the other students.

Nour, who sat in his class, noticed him. She remembered how nervous she had felt when she first came to the school two years earlier. She took her friends and walked towards the bench. "Hi, I'm Nour," she said. "Do you want to play football with us?" Zaid hesitated, then smiled. "I am not very good," he said. "Neither are we," Nour laughed.

By the end of the week, Zaid had learned the names of half of the class. Nour's small act of kindness had taken only a minute, but it changed the way Zaid felt about his new school. On Friday, he said to her, "You made the first day easier. I will do the same for the next new student."

items.title: Tips for First-Time Flyers
text: Flying for the first time can be exciting, but it can also be confusing. A little preparation will make your journey smoother.

Start by arriving at the airport early. You need time to check in, drop your suitcase, pass through security and find your gate. Keep your passport and boarding pass in an easy-to-reach place, because you will show them several times. Remember that there are rules about what you can carry, so check the airline's website before you pack, especially for liquids and sharp objects.

On the plane, listen to the safety instructions and keep your seat belt fastened when the sign is on. If your ears feel blocked during take-off or landing, swallowing or chewing gum can help. Finally, do not panic if you hear unusual sounds or feel small movements. They are a normal part of flying. If you are worried, ask a member of the crew. They are always happy to help.

text: The big screen at the airport showed one word in red: DELAYED. Dina sighed. She was on her way to an English summer course, and her flight would now leave three hours late. She looked around and saw other passengers frowning and checking their watches.

Instead of complaining, she took out a notebook. An old man sitting next to her smiled and asked what she was writing. "New English words," she answered. "I want to use the waiting time." The man, who turned out to be a retired teacher, offered to help. For two hours, they practised speaking English together, and he corrected her pronunciation gently.

When the flight was finally announced, Dina was surprised that the time had passed so quickly. She thanked the old man and walked to the gate. "A delay is only a problem if you let it be," she thought. During the course, her teacher praised her speaking, and Dina remembered the man at the airport.

text: Omar had always been shy, so he was nervous when his teacher asked him to be the guide for his class during their museum visit. "You know the museum well because you come here with your father," she said. Omar swallowed and agreed.

This time, he spoke about the ancient statues the way he talked to his father: slowly and with a smile. He told the story behind each object, and his classmates began to ask questions. By the end of the tour, they clapped for him. Omar was surprised. He had thought he could never speak in front of people, but he had only needed to relax.

items.title: How People Measured Time
text: Today we look at a phone or a watch to know the time, but people lived for thousands of years without them. Early people watched the sun. When the sun was high in the sky, they knew it was midday, and when it went down, they knew the evening was coming.

Later, people invented the sundial. A sundial has a flat plate and a stick that makes a shadow. As the sun moves across the sky, the shadow moves too, and marks on the plate show the hour. The problem was clear: a sundial does not work at night or on a cloudy day.

To solve this problem, people made water clocks. In a water clock, water drips slowly from one container into another, and the level of the water shows how much time has passed. These clocks could be used indoors and at night.

After that, inventors made mechanical clocks with wheels and weights, and later small watches that people could carry. Each invention made time easier to measure and helped people organise their work and their lives.

text: Salma's science club had a special trip: a night visit to an observatory. She had never looked through a real telescope, and she could not sleep the night before. The bus left the city lights behind, and soon the sky above them was full of stars.

When she finally looked, she saw a small bright ball with tiny dots around it. "Those are its moons," the astronomer explained.

Salma stood silently for a long time. Everything she had read in books suddenly felt real. On the way home, she asked herself how many places and worlds were still unknown. items.title: Why the Moon Changes Shape
text: Have you ever noticed that the Moon does not always look the same? Some nights it is a thin curve, some nights it is a half circle, and on other nights it looks like a full bright circle. In fact, the Moon does not change at all. What changes is the part that we can see from Earth.

The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because it reflects the light of the sun. At any time, half of the Moon is lit by the sun, just as half of the Earth has daytime. The Moon moves around the Earth, so we look at the lit half from different angles.

When the lit side faces us, we see a full Moon. When the lit side faces away from us, the Moon is almost invisible. In between, we see only a part of the bright side, which gives us the thin curves and half circles.
The Moon goes through all these shapes in about a month. Because the pattern repeats regularly, people in many cultures have used the Moon to count the days and months.

items.title: Why We Send Robots to Space
text: Space is a dangerous place for humans. There is no air to breathe, the temperatures can be extremely hot or extremely cold, and a journey to another planet can take many months. For these reasons, scientists often send robots instead of people.

Robots have important advantages. They do not need food, water or oxygen, and they can work in places where a human could not survive. If a robot is damaged, no one is hurt, and scientists can learn from the mistake. Robots are also cheaper to send than a team of astronauts, because the spacecraft does not need to carry life support or return to Earth.

Robots can move over the surface of a planet, take photographs, collect samples and send information back to scientists. This information helps us understand how planets are formed and whether life could exist elsewhere.

However, robots cannot think like humans. They follow instructions from scientists on Earth, and sometimes they take a long time to react. That is why many people believe that the best way to explore space is to use robots and humans together.

items.title: Why Hospitality Matters
text: Hospitality means welcoming guests warmly and making them feel at home. In many cultures, including ours, it is a very important value. A guest is offered a drink, a seat in the best place and, often, a meal, even if the visit was not planned.

Hospitality is not only about food. A smile, a kind greeting and careful listening make guests feel respected. A good host also thinks about the guest's comfort. For example, he asks whether the guest needs anything and does not make him feel like a burden.
Good guests also have responsibilities. They should arrive on time, respect the rules of the house and thank the host. They should not stay too long or ask for things that the host cannot provide.

When hosts and guests respect each other, friendships grow stronger. Hospitality also teaches children generosity and good manners. That is why many people say that a society which welcomes its guests is a society that cares about others.

text: When Hana's family moved into the new building, they did not know anyone. For days, the only sounds in the corridor were their own footsteps. Hana's mother was unpacking boxes, and everyone was tired and hungry.

One evening, the doorbell rang. An elderly woman was standing there with a large pot. "I am Mrs. Samia from the flat next door," she said. "I made too much soup, and I thought you might need a hot meal." Hana's mother was so touched that she could hardly speak.

The next day, Hana's mother baked a cake and took it next door. Mrs. Samia invited her in for tea, and the two women talked for an hour. Soon, the children of the building were playing together on the stairs. Hana learned that a small kind act can open a door, and that a stranger can become a friend with a simple bowl of soup.

items.title: What Makes a Good Story
text: We all enjoy a good story, but what makes a story good? Writers usually agree on a few important elements. First, a good story has interesting characters. Readers should care about what happens to them, so the characters must feel real, with strengths and weaknesses.

Second, a good story has a clear plot with a beginning, a middle and an end. At the beginning, we meet the characters and the setting. In the middle, a problem appears, and the characters try to solve it. At the end, the problem is solved in a way that feels logical.

Third, the setting matters. Where and when the events happen can create a mood, such as a quiet village or a stormy night. Good writers also use details, such as sounds and smells, to help the reader imagine the scene.

Finally, a good story often has a message. It does not have to be stated directly. A reader may think about courage, honesty or friendship after finishing it. A story which makes us feel and think is a story we remember.

items.title: Skills Employers Value
text: Good marks help you to get a job interview, but employers often look for more than marks. They want people who have skills that make a team work well. Here are some of the skills that are usually considered most valuable.

The first is communication. An employee must be able to explain ideas clearly, listen to others and write polite emails. The second is teamwork. Most jobs involve working with other people, so being able to share tasks and respect different opinions is essential.

Problem-solving is also very important. Employers prefer people who try to find solutions instead of only reporting problems. Closely related to this is the ability to learn quickly, because technology and methods change all the time.

Finally, employers value responsibility and honesty. They need to know that you will arrive on time, finish your work and tell the truth, even when you make a mistake. You can begin to practise all these skills now, through school projects, clubs and volunteering.

items.title: Being a Good Friend Online
text: Today, many teenagers spend a lot of time chatting with friends online. Online friendships can be fun and useful, but they also need care, just like friendships in real life. A good friend online follows some simple rules.

First, be kind. It is easy to write something hurtful when you cannot see the other person's face. Before you send a message, ask yourself whether you would say the same words directly to your friend. If not, do not send it.

Second, respect privacy. Do not share someone's photos or secrets without permission, and never give away your own personal information, such as your address or your passwords, to people you do not know in real life.

Third, stand up for others. If you see someone being bullied online, do not join in. Support the person and tell a trusted adult. Finally, remember to spend time with friends face to face. Real conversations, games and laughter cannot be replaced by a screen.

text: In recent years, minority-owned businesses in the US have faced both unprecedented opportunities and significant risks. Civil rights activists have long argued that minority groups, such as Blacks and Hispanics, struggle to succeed in business due to lack of access to substantial jus orders from large companies. In response, Congress passed juol laws requiring federal contractors to make efforts to engage minority subcontractors. Many government agencies have set goals to allocate public works contracts to minority businesses. Corporate response has been positive, with contracts for minority businesses increasing from $77 million in 1972 to $1.1 billion in 1977, and projections for the early 1980s estimating over $53 billion annually. However, this growth brings risks for minority businesses. Many are small, requiring large investments in equipment, plants, and staff to handle subcontracted work. If their contracts are reduced, they may face financial difficulties due to fixed expenses. The corporate world can be frustrating for small businesses, with complex bidding 6.:\jo processes that consume time and resources. items.title: How to Improve Your English
text: How you can best improve your English depends particularly on whether or not you live in an English-speaking community. If you hear English spoken every day and mix freely with English speaking people, that is an advantage. On the other hand, it is often confusing to have the whole language poured over you at once. Ideally, a step-by-step course should accompany or lead up to this experience. It will also help a great deal if you can easily get the sort of English books in which you are interested. To read a lot is essential. Read as many books in English as you can, not as study but for pleasure. Do not choose the most difficult books you find with the idea of listing and learning as many new words as possible. Choose what is likely to interest you and be sure in advance that it is not too hard. You should not have to be constantly looking up new words in the dictionary, for that deadens interest and checks real learning. Look up a word here and there but as a general policy try to guess what words mean from the context. You should enjoy the feeling which reading gives of having some command of the language. As you read, you will become more and more familiar with words and sentence patterns you already know; understanding them better and better as you meet them in more and more contexts, some of which may differ only slightly from others

items.title: Taking Care of Your Heart
text: Our body has many organs which do their functions properly. Each one has a specific job to do to survive. For example, your heart, a tireless pump working faithfully day and night, is vital to your very existence. But what happens when this vital organ is starved of the oxygen it needs? A heart attack, also known as a myocardial infarction, occurs when blood flow to a part of the heart muscle is severely reduced or cut off completely. This disrupts the heart’s ability to pump blood effectively, threatening your health and even your life. The culprit behind most heart attacks is atherosclerosis, a gradual narrowing of the coronary arteries. These arteries supply blood rich in oxygen to the heart muscle. Over time, fatty deposits called plaque buildup on the artery walls, restrict blood flow. A piece of plaque may rupture, triggering the formation of a blood clot that can completely block the artery. This blockage starves the heart muscle of oxygen, leading to cell death and a heart attack. Symptoms of a heart attack can vary from person to person. The classic image of someone clutching their chest in pain is common, but discomfort can also manifest as pain in the arm, shoulder, jaw, back, or even nausea and lightheadedness. Recognizing these diverse symptoms and seeking immediate medical attention is crucial. Early intervention can minimize heart damage and improve your chances of a full recovery. Thankfully, there are steps you can take to reduce your risk of a heart attack. Maintaining a healthy lifestyle is key. This includes eating a balanced diet low in saturated fats, exercising regularly, managing stress, and maintaining a healthy weight. Additionally, controlling conditions like high blood pressure and cholesterol can significantly decrease your risk. By understanding the causes and symptoms of heart attacks, and by prioritizing a heart- healthy lifestyle, you can empower yourself to take charge of your cardiovascular health

items.title: Scientific Research
text: Scientific research is a systematic way of studying the world to discover new knowledge. Scientists use research to understand natural phenomena and solve problems. The process usually begins with a question or a problem that needs investigation. Next, the scientist forms a hypothesis, which is a possible explanation that can be tested. - After that, experiments or observations are carried out to collect data. The data are then analyzed carefully to see whether the hypothesis is correct or not. Another important step in scientific research is reviewing the results. Scientists discuss their findings with other experts who carefully check the research. This process is called peer review. It helps make sure that the research is accurate and reliable before it is published. Peer review also helps scientists improve their work and correct any mistakes. Finally, scientists share their results with others through reports, articles, or presentations. Scientific research is important because it helps improve technology, medicine, and our understanding of the universe

text: Artificial Intelligence (AJ) refers to the simulation of human intelligence in machines that are programmed to think and learn like humans. items.title: Food Insecurity
text: About 349 million people across 79 countries are facing acute food insecurity -up from 287 million in 2021. The global community must not fail on its promise to end hunger and malnutrition by 2030. Many innovations that were once heavily supported and publicized, such as fish-protein concentrate and protein from algae grown on petroleum substrates, have fallen by the wayside. The proposals themselves were technically feasible, but they proved to be economically unviable and to yield food products culturally unacceptable to their consumers. Recent innovations such as opaque-2 maize seems promising, but it is too early to predict its ultimate fate. Marine Life 259 Despite having extensive governmental support, these unsuccessful innovations often have not been technologically adapted or culturally acceptable to the people for whom they had been developed. A successful new technology, therefore, must fit the entire sociocultural system in which it is to find a place. Security of crop yield, practicality of storage, taste and costs should be taken into consideration. For example, the better protein quality in bread made from opaque-2 maize will be of only limited benefit to a family on the margin of subsistence if the new maize is not culturally acceptable or is more likely to be attacked by insects. The adoption of new. food technologies depends on more than these technical and cultural considerations; economic factors and governmental policies also strongly influence the ultimate success of any innovation. Some economists exaggerate in claiming that profitability is the key factor guiding technical change and disregard the substantial effects of culture. Most technological innovations in agriculture can be fully used and adopted only by large landowners if they believe that the innovations will increase their incomes even if they harm sectors of the population and reduce the availability of food in a country

items.title: Five Kinds of Memory
text: Most people worry about forgetting things as they get older. Do you know that we have different kinds of memories? What most people think of as a memory is, in fact, five different categories of memory. Remembering things from the past depends on two categories of memory: remote and recent memory. If you can’t remember things about your last birthday, you are having a problem with your remote memory. If you can’t remember what you ate for lunch yesterday, that’s a problem with your recent memory. When we take a test, we need to draw on our semantic memories. That’s the sum of our acquired knowledge, or we want to remember to do or use something in the future. Here we use our immediate and prospective memories. Many people think that developing a bad memory is inevitable as we get older, but this is actually not correct. Of our five kinds of memory, immediate; remote and prospective don’t degrade with age. To have good memories, we need to do some activities like learning new things or even doing crossword puzzles. Regular physical activity is useful to have a better blood supply to the brain. The only thing to avoid is stress. When we are stressed, our bodies release a hormone called cortisol, which is harmful to our brain cells and our memories. Reducing stress through meditation, exercise, or other activities can help to preserve our mental abilities

items.title: Our Five Senses
text: Sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste are the five senses we have, through which we learn, see, hear and discover the world around us. Many people believe that our senses work separately, but in fact they collaborate together and work as a team to enable the mind to understand its surroundings. But, do all creatures have five senses? Some people may have six senses. A sixth sense could be predicting something without using the known five senses. Researchers have discovered that some dolphins have seven senses. Dolphins can feel electricity produced by the heart beats of other sea creatures. This could help dolphins to find their next victim to hunt as their meal. This seventh sense may also help them to navigate using the Earth’s magnetic field. Dolphins also use their eyesight and sonar to feel what is around them. The researchers performed a study on two dolphins to make sure that they really have the seventh sense. Experiments tested what kinds of electricity the dolphins could feel. They felt two kinds, direct current and alternating current. They were better at sensing direct current. All sea creatures produce direct current electricity. Being able to discover this means dolphins can feel how near other fish are to them. Dolphins could use this to hunt and eat, even if they cannot see or hear well, or if they cannot use their other senses

Although they lived during the early years of human existence, they have acquired exceptional data. Ancient Egypt has been a major contributor to modern day medicine, for they have given knowledge of hygiene, surgery and the uses of herbs. The Egyptians’ need to be clean and hygienic has greatly influenced many people in this time and age, preventing what could cause medical damage. In the modern-day world, there are still some remedies and treatments practiced that was discovered by the Egyptians. Some herbal and natural remedies used in modern day time include mint, garlic and Aloe Vera, while their other herbal medicines provided a base for our everyday UNIT ) (322) medicines, such as antibiotics and pain killers. When it came to pain killers, it is recorded that the ancient Egyptians had an understanding and used natural remedies to control pain long before Europeans figured out the natural powers of such herbs. They understood and used herbs and natural elements to protect themselves from disease and parasites. In Egypt, they treated worms with pomegranates and garlic, later proven by modern medical studies that the ancient Egyptians were absolutely right to treat worms with them. This is because; modern scientists confirmed that the contents in pomegranate and garlic can actually kill worms. As for everyday remedies, the Egyptians also used the powers of the Aloe Vera plant to calm burning skin and mint to relieve severe pain. items.title: Clocks and Time
text: Clocks are used to measure and show the time. Clocks are used so that people can agree on the time. People use clocks to measure units of time that are shorter than natural units. Natural units are the day, the month, and the year. The clock is a very old invention. Sundials were used in ancient times, Sundials work by measuring shadows that are cast by the sun. Candle clocks were used a very long time ago. Candle clocks work by measuring the time it takes for the wax to melt. Hourglasses are similar to candle clocks because they also measure the time it takes for something to happen. Hourglasses work by measuring the time it takes for sand to pour through a small opening into a glass. Mechanical clocks appeared in the 13 century in Europe. They work with a system of moving gears. The gears always move at the same speed. Pendulum clocks work with a swinging weight. : 326 { The swinging weight is called a pendulum. The pendulum makes the clock parts move. Now people typically use mechanical clocks or digital clocks. Digital clocks show numbers on a screen. The numbers represent the time. Some people use auditory clocks. Auditory clocks use language to tell the time aloud. Computers also use internal clocks in order to work properly. Clocks are everywhere: in homes, schools, offices, and public places. People go to work and return home according to the clock. School days start and end according to the clock. Airplanes take off and land according to the clock. It is fun to imagine a world without clocks

items.title: The History of False Teeth
text: People have been wearing false teeth of one kind or another for a long time. The Etruscans made the first false teeth in 700 BC, but their knowledge of false teeth was forgotten for many years and no one knew how to make them. When people’s teeth fell out — often when they were still young — they looked old. Even Queen Elizabeth I lost her front teeth and had to put pieces of cloth under her lips to fill out her face. At one time in England, dentists pulled out people’s teeth in public, without giving them anything to stop the pain. Sometimes one of the dentists’ assistants hit a drum loudly so that people in the crowd could not hear the cries of pain. It wasn’t until the 17 century that dentists started to make false teeth again. Only rich people could afford false teeth which were usually made of ivory, gold or silver. Sometimes, dentists used other people’s teeth (usually poor people’s). Poor people sold their teeth to the rich so that they could buy food and clothing. Towards the end of the 19'* century, cheap celluloid teeth were introduced. But, they caught fire very easily and a number of men were badly burned when their teeth caught fire while they were smoking cigarettes. In the 20" century plastic false teeth were introduced. In the future we will probably not need false teeth because our teeth will be so healthy

text: In 1911, Charlie Chaplin, a penniless music-hall artist, left England for America. His future was uncertain, but he believed it couldn’t be unhappier than his past. He began to develop the character of the tramp that is connected with his name. He borrowed ideas from many sources. He used his bowler hat to signal secret messages and his walking stick allowed him to cause confusion and punish his enemy from a distance. He got the idea of his famous fat-footed walk from a London taxi driver who had sore feet. Inside the tramp’s clothes, the audience saw a human being who was poor, but dreamt of being rich. The audience would be moved by this, but before they had time to reach for their handkerchiefs, Charlie’s feet would get in the way and make them laugh instead. Charlie was the master of mime and as an acrobat, he used to perform dangerous stunts. In 1919, he performed his film and wanted to write about his experiences. items.title: Online Learning
text: Online learning has become a vital part of education, especially in recent years. It provides students with the flexibility to learn from anywhere with an internet connection. This method of education uses digital platforms to deliver lessons, assignments, and exams, making it accessible to a wide range of learners. One of the main advantages of online learning is that it allows students to learn at their own pace. They can revisit lectures and materials as many times as needed, ensuring they understand the content fully. Additionally, online learning offers a variety of resources, including videos, interactive quizzes, and discussion forums, which support different learning styles. Another significant benefit is the convenience it offers. Students no longer need to commute to a physical classroom, saving time and allowing for a more flexible schedule. This is especially helpful for those with busy lives or other commitments. Furthermore, online learning connects students with educators and peers from around the world, promoting a diverse and inclusive learning environment. Despite its advantages, online learning also has challenges. It requires self-discipline and motivation, as students must manage their time effectively. Technical issues and lack of access to reliable internet can also pose problems. In summary, online learning is a powerful tool that offers flexibility, a variety of resources, and global connections, but it requires dedication and reliable technology to be effective

items.title: How Glass Is Made
text: Glass is a special compound made from sand melted at a very high temperature with the help of catalysts. Silicate, the main component of sand, is heated until it becomes red-hot. When it has been sufficiently heated, it is wound around a blowing pipe. Specially trained workers, who have learned to control their breathing, blow cups, bowls, vases, and bottles from the heated silicate. These workers must avoid mistakes, because any wrong technique could damage their lungs or seriously harm their internal organs. Glass makers train for years before achieving the status of master craftsmen. They join the glass factory from a young age, working for minimal pay as apprentices. They quickly learn the trade and become ordinary craftsmen. With practice and experience, they may eventually become master craftsmen. If a particular cup or vase requires a special rim or design, the master craftsman handles it himself. Otherwise, mass-produced glasses may be molded in die-casts. Great patience is needed to make glass. After it is shaped and left aside to cool, it must be given enough time to contract. If it is not “aged” sufficiently, it will crack and fall apart

items.title: Simplifying English Spelling
text: Over the years people have tried to simplify the spelling of English words. Unlike other languages, English spells the same sounds in very different ways. For example, there is’ “Joan” but “phone”, and the letters “ough” are pronounced differently: “though”, “through”, “cough” and “enough”. The great Irish writer, George Bernard Shaw, was very interested in making English spelling more logical. In 1906 one of the richest men in America, Andrew Carnegie, started the Simplified Spelling Board. This board was a group of people whose plan was to make the spelling of words nearer to the way they sounded. For example, the word “though” would be spelt “tho” whereas “through” would become “thru”. The idea was taken to the American president — Theodore Roosevelt — who thought it was a very good one. He told the government printer to use the simplified spelling on all government letters. Many people disliked the new simpler spelling. The British — who probably thought they owned the English language — were particularly angry. More importantly, when American politicians discussed the plan, they did not like it. Because Roosevelt did not want to have a problem with the politicians, he changed his plans and told the printer to go back to the old way of spelling
